soil-agri-059.title: Keeping topsoil in place and fertile
soil-agri-059.text: Farmers have practiced soil conservation for millennia. The ancient Phoenicians already plowed along the contour on slopes of two to ten percent. Soil conservation means preventing two kinds of loss. One is topsoil carried away by erosion. The other is fertility worn down by overuse, {{ref:soil-chem-001}}, salinization or chemical contamination. The stakes can be total. Deforestation typically brings large-scale erosion and lost nutrients, and sometimes complete {{ref:soil-env-072}}. Salinity alone is estimated to affect about one third of the earth's arable land. It is left behind when irrigation water evaporates, or when it rises from shallow saline water tables. The techniques include crop rotation, {{ref:soil-agri-066}}, conservation tillage and rows of trees planted against the wind, and each works on erosion and fertility together. Organic matter pays off in water: each one percent increase in soil organic matter helps soil hold 20,000 gallons more water per acre. Governments joined in on a large scale after the Dust Bowl, starting in Franklin D. Roosevelt's first 100 days in 1933. In Europe, the Common Agricultural Policy promotes reduced tillage, crops kept over winter to cover the soil, plant residues and grass margins. Yet erosion is not only a farming problem. How land is valued is a governance hurdle, so solving erosion also takes political and economic action, and cultural change can shift it.

soil-agri-066.title: Cover crops: plants grown to protect, not to sell
soil-agri-066.text: Some crops are never meant for market. A cover crop is planted to cover the soil rather than to be harvested. Farmers often sow it off-season, after the cash crop comes in, and let it grow over winter. Often its only job is to fight erosion. Its leaves shield the surface and scatter the energy of falling raindrops. It slows water flowing over the ground and lets more of it soak in, while its roots anchor the soil and open new pores. Below ground it stirs up microbial activity, which makes more nitrogen available to the next crop and can lift yields. A meta-analysis of 102 field studies measured these effects against bare or fallow ground. Saturated hydraulic conductivity, the ease with which water flows through soaked soil, rose about 106%. Topsoil organic carbon rose about 10% and nitrogen about 20%. Microbial biomass carbon climbed about 20%, and particulate organic carbon nearly 50%. The benefits come with trade-offs. A cover crop may use water the next crop needs, or leave yields unchanged, especially in semi-arid regions or when it is killed at the wrong time. Before the cash crop goes in, farmers end it by mowing, tilling, discing, rolling or spraying herbicide. In all, cover crops touch erosion, fertility, soil quality, water, weeds, pests, diseases, biodiversity and wildlife. They also act as nurse crops that help the main crop survive.

soil-agri-063.title: Soil management: keeping fields productive for decades
soil-agri-063.text: Conventional and organic farms alike need soil management to stay productive over decades. It means applying operations, practices and treatments that protect soil and improve how it performs, from its fertility to its mechanical behavior. It takes in soil conservation, soil amendment and the pursuit of optimal soil health. Organic farming leans on it hardest, since soil health supplies almost all of its fertility and pest control. Controlling traffic on the surface limits compaction, which can cut aeration and water infiltration. Cover crops keep soil anchored and covered off-season. Rotations alternate high- and low-residue crops to keep plant material on the surface against erosion. Conventional tillage disturbs soil most deeply, while reduced tillage and no-till keep residues in place. Fertilizers add nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur and potassium, but they often acidify soils; potassium fertilizer is the exception. Organic matter added to the surface can raise the carbon stored in soil and the abundance and diversity of soil microbes. Project Drawdown counts improved nutrient management, {{ref:soil-agri-065}} and regenerative agriculture among the soil steps for slowing climate change.

soil-agri-073.title: Terraces: staircases carved into hillsides
soil-agri-073.text: On steep ground, farmers have long cut the slope into a staircase. Each step is a terrace, a flat surface carved into a hill or mountainside for growing crops. Terraced fields reduce both erosion and surface runoff, and they can hold irrigated crops such as rice. Terracing is more common on small farms. Terraced paddies carry rice, wheat and barley across much of Asia, the Mediterranean Basin, Africa and South America. Terrace farming in the Levant goes back as early as the 4th millennium BCE. Terraces in the Yemen Highlands date from the start of the Bronze Age, in the 3rd millennium BC. In the Andes, the Wari and others built terraces called andenes before 1000 AD, to use shallow soil efficiently and irrigate crops; the Inca later adopted them. Luminescence dating shows a major burst of Mediterranean terrace building in the later Middle Ages, around AD 1100–1600. Some dates remain unsettled. Scholars disagree on when the terraces of the Jerusalem Mountains were built, from the Bronze Age to the Roman and Byzantine periods. Luminescence dates there may reflect later modification. Long-term moisture management by terracing can even create anthraquic Anthrosols.

soil-agri-140.title: Agroforestry: farming with the forest as a model
soil-agri-140.text: The forester John Bene coined the word agroforestry in 1973, but the practices it names are millennia old. Agroforestry is a land use system that integrates trees with crops or pasture. It is managed to optimize the interactions among plants and animals, with the forest as its model, which makes it applied agroecology. Groundcover protects depleted soil from erosion, and trees slow runoff and evaporation so more water soaks in. Nitrogen-fixing plants such as legumes can restore soil nitrogen fertility. Carbon can build up in both soil and woody biomass. The USDA lists five temperate practices: alley cropping, forest farming, riparian forest buffers, silvopasture and {{ref:soil-agri-061}}. In Honduras, the Quesungual system replaced slash-and-burn hillside farming, whose exposed soil washed away. It keeps nitrogen-fixing trees that cut erosion and hold moisture. In 2025, 91 countries and areas reported 55.4 million hectares under agroforestry, most of it in Asia.

soil-agri-061.title: Windbreaks: rows of trees that hold the soil down
soil-agri-061.text: A few rows of trees can change the climate of a whole field. A windbreak, also called a shelterbelt, is one or more rows of trees or shrubs planted to shelter land from the wind and protect soil from erosion. Shelterbelts run perpendicular to the prevailing wind, while woodlots are more extensive areas of woodland. Behind a windbreak, the wind is slowest at about 3 to 5 times the windbreak's height downwind, then recovers. Evergreens protect all year, but deciduous trees may be enough if they are in leaf while the soil is bare. Farmers plant windbreaks to cut wind erosion of loess, and very light soils need them in dry weather. Besides sharply reducing erosion, they reduce evapotranspiration, improve the microclimate for crops, shelter beneficial birds, sequester carbon and improve the landscape. They separate fields and shield them from pesticide spray drift. They hold snow on fields, where it supplies water as it melts in spring. With woodlots, they help fix the soil against {{ref:soil-env-072}}.

soil-agri-072.title: Strip farming: alternating bands that act as dams
soil-agri-072.text: Where a slope is too steep, or no other method can prevent erosion, farmers turn to strips. Strip farming, also called strip cropping, divides a field into long, narrow strips that alternate in a crop rotation. Strips of close-sown hay, wheat or forage, serving mainly as cover crops, alternate with row crops such as corn, soybeans, cotton or sugar beets. Laid out along the approximate contour, the sod strips act as natural dams. They slow water and hold back soil washing from the cultivated strips. Strips are usually 25 feet (7.6 m) to 75 feet (23 m) wide, and 50 feet (15 m) suits most machinery. On the dry-farmed Great Plains and Canadian Prairies, strips run at right angles to the wind. Contour strip cropping, used mainly on gentle slopes, makes the protective strips wider so they intercept runoff. In strip intercropping, narrower contiguous strips suit machinery and let neighboring crops benefit from each other. In the Midwestern United States, strips of native plants, described in {{ref:soil-agri-142}}, serve as contour buffers and edge-of-field filters that build soil health and curb erosion.

soil-agri-067.title: Green manures: cover crops that feed the soil
soil-agri-067.text: Some cover crops are grown not to guard the soil but to feed it. Fertility-building cover crops are called green manures, and they are often plowed under before they mature. Legumes do this best. Their roots are nodulated by bacteria such as Bradyrhizobium, which fix nitrogen from the air into ammonium. A leguminous cover crop can often supply all the nitrogen a crop needs. This ability to stand in for chemical nitrogen fertilizer is called fertilizer replacement value. It matters beyond the farm. Nitrogen fertilizer lost to waterways causes {{ref:soil-env-020}}, as in the Gulf of Mexico's summer dead zone of over 22,000 square kilometers. Some scientists see biological nitrogen fixation, mainly through cover crops, as the only alternative to fossil-fuel-dependent industrial nitrogen fixation for future food production. Other nutrients can benefit too. In Nigeria, a velvet bean cover crop increased soil phosphorus availability after rock phosphate was applied.

soil-agri-065.title: Conservation agriculture: disturb little, cover always
soil-agri-065.text: Tillage was once thought to raise fertility. It is now seen to destroy organic matter and cause erosion and crusting. Conservation agriculture is one response. The FAO defines it as a farming system that prevents loss of arable land and regenerates degraded land. It rests on minimal soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and diverse plant species. Plowing is eliminated or greatly reduced, as in no-till farming, and mulch or cover crops keep the ground covered. The mulch slows runoff, softens raindrop impact, and keeps soil moister and warmer than yearly tillage would. With less plowing, earthworms thrive and a mull-like agricultural humus form called agri-mull develops. Mineral fertilizer is cut to the crop's strict requirements and is sometimes unnecessary. No-till can save producers 30% to 40% of their time and labor. The drawbacks are real. Benefits can take many years, new planters or drills cost money, and in developing countries the residues it needs are traditionally fed to livestock. With regenerative and organic agriculture, it counts as sustainable agriculture.

soil-agri-076.title: Soil stabilization: engineering weak ground for roads
soil-agri-076.text: A road is only as strong as the ground beneath it. Soil stabilization is any physical, chemical, mechanical or biological method, alone or combined, of altering a natural soil to meet an engineering purpose. It raises the bearing capacity, tensile strength and overall performance of unstable subsoils, sands and waste materials, chiefly to strengthen roads. Traditional binders for a road base are bitumen, tar emulsions, asphalt, cement and lime, along with fly ash, cement kiln dust and tree resins. Each has drawbacks. Bitumen is not environmentally friendly and turns brittle when dry, and Portland cement is often expensive. Newer stabilizers include enzymes, surfactants, synthetic and bio-polymers, fiber reinforcement and chloride salts. Some form water-repelling layers that keep out water and frost. Many so-called green products work like soap powder, only lubricating and realigning the soil without binding it. Many new approaches rely instead on clay's own binding properties. The Deep Mixing Method injects through a small probe to strengthen weak or loose soil strata and repair sinkholes. Adding stabilizing materials can also limit a soil's ability to shrink and swell.

soil-agri-062.title: Fewer pesticides, healthier soil
soil-agri-062.text: Pesticides do not vanish after spraying. They can contaminate soil, nearby vegetation and water for a long time, and they affect soil structure and its living and nonliving makeup. Cutting their use is one way to protect soil. Alternatives include irradiation, cultivation methods, biological controls such as pheromones and microbial pesticides, genetic engineering and disrupting insect breeding. Composted yard waste has also controlled pests. Researchers have studied policy tools too, among them differentiated taxation schemes.

soil-agri-060.title: Soil-conservation farming and its critics
soil-agri-060.text: Repeated plowing degrades soil and kills its beneficial fungi and earthworms. Soil-conservation farming avoids that harm by combining no-till, green manures and other soil-enhancing practices. No-till and cover crops hold nitrogen and other nutrients, raising soil organic matter. Advocates say it can revive damaged soil and minimize erosion at lower labor and cost. They add that it can remove the need for nitrogen fertilizer or fungicide and protect crops in drought or flood. Critics disagree. They call no-till and related methods impractical and costly, cite advantages of conventional tillage in some settings, and say no-till complicates pest control and residue management.

soil-agri-064.title: How farm soils can warm or cool the climate
soil-agri-064.text: Farm soil can work on either side of the climate ledger. Management can emit nitrous oxide and carbon, or store carbon dioxide in the soil, described in {{ref:soil-env-108}}. Fertilizer use, irrigation and tillage all contribute to nitrous oxide emissions, and soil management accounts for over half of the agriculture sector's emissions. Using biochar may cut nitrous oxide emissions from soils by an average of 54%. Converting natural land to farmland releases carbon. How much carbon a soil can store depends on climate, land-use history and management. Cropland could sequester 0.5–1.2 Pg C/year, and grazing and pasture land 0.3–0.7 Pg C/year. Storage rises with more biomass inputs, smaller losses of that stored carbon and a longer mean residence time for that carbon. No-till, residue mulching, cover cropping and crop rotation significantly enhance carbon storage in soil. All four are more common in organic than in conventional farming.

soil-agri-069.title: How cover crops steer rain into the ground
soil-agri-069.text: Cover crops change the path rain takes through a field. Their biomass shields the surface from rain, and their roots open pores that let water filter down instead of running off. Greater infiltration can improve soil water storage and aquifer recharge. Because they curb erosion, cover crops also reduce the rate and amount of water draining off fields, a risk to waterways downstream. Where water is scarce, cover crops used as mulch shade and cool the surface, reducing evaporation.

soil-agri-071.title: Cover crops that trap pests and fight disease
soil-agri-071.text: White mustard and radish set a trap. Nematodes enter the roots of these resistant plants but cannot reproduce there, and their populations fall by 70–99%. Cover crops can break pest and disease cycles, lure pests away as trap crops and attract the pests' natural enemies. Mustards and other Brassicaceae suppress fungal diseases with toxic chemicals, released as compounds in the plants called glucosinolates break down. Grasses, legumes and brassicas also raise soil organic matter and microbial activity, making cash crops more resilient to insect pests and pathogens. Findings on predators and pests are mixed, though, so effects depend on the cover crop and its management.

soil-agri-070.title: Smothering weeds with a cover crop
soil-agri-070.text: A cover crop fights weeds twice: by competing with them while it grows, and by smothering or poisoning them after it dies. Flattened on the surface, it forms a nearly impenetrable mat that blocks light and cuts weed germination. This is the smother effect. Some cover crops also release compounds that inhibit other plants, the process called allelopathy. Rye, hairy vetch, red clover, sorghum-sudangrass and mustards all do this. After termination, yellow sweetclover residues held weeds 75–97% below their levels in fallow systems. Rye residues used as mulch gave 80% to 95% control of early-season broadleaf weeds.

soil-agri-075.title: Contour trenches that catch the rain
soil-agri-075.text: On a dry hillside, rain that runs straight off is rain lost. Contour trenching digs continuous trenches along a slope's contour to conserve water and soil and raise crop yields. Each trench catches water flowing downhill so it soaks into the soil. Crops between the trenches draw on this subsoil reserve during the drier growing season, so they suffer less from later water shortage. Fertile particles are no longer lost to water and wind erosion. Each trench must hold all the water, with its upslope side protected by grass, shrubs or fabric. It is one of the techniques used to reverse {{ref:soil-env-072}}.

soil-agri-079.title: The 1936 law that paid farmers to save soil
soil-agri-079.text: The Supreme Court declared the Agricultural Adjustment Act unconstitutional, and Congress passed the Soil Conservation and Domestic Allotment Act of 1936 in its wake. This US federal law let the government pay farmers to cut production in order to conserve soil and prevent erosion. It amended and renamed the Soil Conservation Act of 1935, to preserve soil fertility and reduce the exploitation and unprofitable use of national soil resources. Landlords now had to share the payments with the sharecroppers and tenants who worked their land. On the Dust Bowl's high plains, the act directed conservation work: educating farmers and planting trees and native grass.

soil-agri-081.title: Lynchets: the stepped hillsides of ancient Britain
soil-agri-081.text: A lynchet is an earth terrace on a hillside, typical of the ancient field systems of the British Isles. The word is the diminutive of lynch, an old term for an agricultural terrace. Lynchets often run in vertical rows, called strip lynchets, mostly in southern Britain near Iron Age forts and older earthworks. The traditional theory credits long plowing, which makes soil slip downslope. That builds a positive lynchet where the surface rises and a negative lynchet where it drops. Yet the size, spacing and number of rows show that many were man-made, most likely dug to make the most of land for farming.

soil-agri-074.title: Terracettes: the catsteps of steep pastures
soil-agri-074.text: Steep pastures are often ribbed with small, irregular steps. These terracettes, also called catsteps or cattle terracing, are roughly parallel, step-like ridges on a steep hillside. How they form is disputed. Darwin (1904) thought grazing animals made them, and trampling sheep or cattle do worsen soil creep and surface erosion. But some end abruptly at rock faces or soil changes, and livestock trails cut across others. Geomorphologists doubt animals alone could form such regular steps. Soil processes offer another explanation. Saturated soil swells, then shrinks as it dries, so particles creep slowly downhill; freeze–thaw and heating–cooling cycles can do the same.

soil-agri-080.title: The Great Plains Shelterbelt: 220 million trees against dust
soil-agri-080.text: In 1934, Franklin D. Roosevelt answered the Dust Bowl's dust storms with trees. The Great Plains Shelterbelt was a US project to plant windbreaks across the Great Plains states. Trees around farms were meant to cut wind speed and soil moisture loss. The first tree, an Austrian pine, went into an Oklahoma farm in 1935. Farmers were paid to plant and tend native trees such as red cedar and green ash along fence rows. By 1942, 30,233 shelterbelts held 220 million trees over 18,600 square miles (48,000 km2). They filled a 100-mile wide zone from North Dakota's Canadian border to the Brazos River in Texas. By 2010 many were old and declining, and federal grants funded their renovation in Kansas, North Dakota, South Dakota and Nebraska.

soil-agri-141.title: Check dams: small barriers that slow the flow
soil-agri-141.text: A low wall of rocks across a ditch can slow it down. A check dam is a small, sometimes temporary dam built across a swale, ditch or waterway to counter erosion by slowing the water. Builders use rocks, gravel, logs, hay bales or sandbags, and the dam is usually less than 2 to 3 feet high. It flattens the channel gradient, so the flow slows, more water soaks in and erosion drops. Coarse and medium sediment settles behind it while finer grains pass through, but it is not mainly a sediment trap. In arid areas, check dams are built to increase groundwater recharge.

soil-agri-068.title: Catch crops: grabbing leftover nitrogen between harvests
soil-agri-068.text: After a harvest, surplus nitrogen from the last crop often lingers in the soil. A catch crop is a fast-growing crop, a type of cover crop, grown between two successive main crops. Usually a fast-growing cereal, it takes up that leftover nitrogen before leaching, denitrification or volatilization can carry it off. The nitrogen returns to the soil when the crop is worked in as green manure or decomposes. Its residue roughens the surface against splash and runoff, and its decaying roots leave biopores, channels that increase infiltration. Sowing date, harvest date and tillage decide its benefit, and sowing later than recommended reduces its nitrogen uptake.

soil-agri-078.title: Magnesium chloride: a salty answer to road dust
soil-agri-078.text: Magnesium chloride pulls water out of the air at a relative humidity of just 32%. Spread on unpaved roads and dusty sites, it keeps the surface damp and binds gravel and clay particles to the road, so fine particles stay grounded. It works better in humid than in arid climates, and its chief benefit is lower maintenance costs for gravel roads. Its use is controversial. Advocates cite cleaner air and safer roads. Yet the dissolved salts reach groundwater and surface water, where chloride above 250 mg/L is regulated. Salts building up in roadside soils harm plants, partly by raising the osmotic pressure of the soil solution.

soil-agri-077.title: Geogrids and geocells: holding soil grains in place
soil-agri-077.text: A soil layer grows stronger when its particles cannot move. Mechanical soil stabilization confines them, for example with geogrids or three-dimensional geocells. Geogrids confine aggregate by interlocking with it. Geocells hold it by the hoop stress of their cell walls, the tension running around each cell. On Swedish forest roads, geocell-reinforced sections markedly raised bearing capacity and reduced permanent deformation under repeated traffic. Locally sourced infill may perform as well as or better than imported crushed aggregate. Better drainage, for instance with stone mattresses, also stabilizes roads by removing excess pore water and spreading loads.

soil-agri-142.title: Prairie strips: a tenth of a field that guards the rest
soil-agri-142.text: Giving 10% of a corn field to native plants can reduce sediment movement by 95%. Prairie strips are strips of native perennial vegetation placed within row-crop fields to protect soil and water and support biodiversity. The same set-aside cuts runoff losses of phosphorus by 90% and of nitrogen by 85%. Native prairie plants stabilize soil and concentrate more organic carbon in it than corn and soybean do. Farmers place the strips as contour buffers and edge-of-field filters, often on hard-to-farm areas. They also supported twice as many aphid-eating insects as soybean fields.

openers.soil-conservation: Topsoil can be lost in two ways: carried off by erosion, or stripped of its fertility by overuse, acidification, salinization or chemical contamination. This chapter is about preventing both. Its tools range from the humble to the monumental: a crop sown only to cover the ground, rows of trees planted against the wind, long narrow strips of alternating crops, and flat steps cut into a mountainside like a staircase. Some approaches join many practices into whole farming systems that barely disturb the soil, keep it covered and mix plant species. Engineers have their own version, altering a natural soil until it can serve an engineering purpose such as carrying a road.

reviews.soil-conservation: Soil conservation fights two losses, topsoil to erosion and fertility to overuse, and every tool in this chapter targets one or both. Some work by covering the ground: cover crops shield the surface and open pores, green manures and catch crops hold nitrogen, and conservation agriculture keeps mulch on fields that are barely disturbed. Others reshape the land or tame the wind, from ancient terraces and lynchets to contour trenches, check dams, crop strips and the 220 million trees of the Great Plains Shelterbelt. Governments joined in after the Dust Bowl, paying farmers to conserve soil, while engineers strengthened soils for roads with binders, geocells and dust-binding salts. The same choices reach the climate, since soil management can emit nitrous oxide and carbon or store carbon in the soil.
